bounds.hint: Write down the interval that could have rounded to each given measurement.
notes: A measurement rounded to the nearest unit represents values half a unit below up to, but not including, half a unit above the stated value. Use the actual rounding unit: it may be 10, 0.1 or another amount.

For a largest possible positive quotient, use the largest numerator and smallest denominator. For a smallest quotient, reverse those choices. Decide which extremes increase the expression before calculating.
Keep the bounds unrounded during the calculation. Distinguish an upper bound from an attainable maximum when the endpoint is excluded.

grouped-mean.hint: Represent each class by its midpoint, then take account of how often that midpoint occurs.
notes: Calculate each class midpoint as (lower endpoint + upper endpoint) ÷ 2. Multiply each midpoint by its frequency.
The estimated mean is Σ(f × midpoint) ÷ Σf. Dividing by the number of classes gives the wrong weighting.
It is an estimate because the individual values within each class are unknown.

histogram.hint: Compare the widths of the class intervals before deciding what the bar heights represent.
notes: In a histogram, frequency is represented by area. Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
For an incomplete histogram, use a bar with known frequency to establish the vertical scale. Then use width × density for a missing frequency.
For only part of an interval, use the corresponding fraction of its area; this assumes the values are spread uniformly within that interval.

cumulative.hint: Use running totals and connect each total to the upper endpoint of its interval.
notes: Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary. Start at the lower boundary of the first class with cumulative frequency zero.
Read the median at N/2, the lower quartile at N/4 and the upper quartile at 3N/4. Read horizontally to the curve, then vertically to the value axis.
To count values between two cutoffs, subtract their cumulative frequencies.

quartiles.hint: Locate the middle half of the data before comparing its spread.
notes: Order raw data first. The interquartile range is upper quartile − lower quartile; the ordinary range uses the maximum and minimum.
A box plot shows the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum. Use the median to compare typical values and the interquartile range to compare consistency.
For grouped or graphical data, quartiles are estimates. Read the axis scale carefully.

scatter.hint: Look at the overall direction and closeness of the points, rather than joining them.
notes: Positive correlation means larger values of one variable tend to accompany larger values of the other; negative correlation means the opposite.
Draw a line of best fit through the centre of the pattern, with a reasonable balance of points on each side.
Use the line for estimates within the observed range. Predictions far outside that range are less reliable, and correlation does not establish causation.

pie-chart.hint: Connect the sector angle to the same fraction of the total frequency.
notes: Sector angle ÷ 360° = category frequency ÷ total frequency. Rearrange for the quantity requested.
Check that all sector angles add to 360°. A larger angle does not necessarily mean more people when comparing charts with different totals.

stem-leaf.hint: Use the key to establish the value represented by each stem and leaf.
notes: Keep the stems ordered and arrange the leaves in each row in ascending order. Include a key that specifies the place value.
Count every leaf, including repeats. The ordered diagram can then be used to locate the median, range or requested proportion.

probability-tree.hint: At each stage, ask whether the first outcome changes what remains for the next one.
notes: Branches leaving one point must have probabilities that add to 1. Without replacement, both the total number available and the relevant category count may change.
Multiply probabilities along one complete path. Add the probabilities of separate paths that satisfy the requested event.
For “at least one”, consider 1 − P(none) when that is shorter.

probability.hint: Describe exactly which outcomes satisfy the event before calculating their probability.
notes: For equally likely outcomes, probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes. Check that the outcomes really are equally likely.
Add probabilities for mutually exclusive alternatives. Multiply for successive events, adjusting the second probability if the first outcome changes the situation.
“Not” often suggests a complement: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Keep fractions exact until the end.

venn.hint: Start with the overlap, then fill the regions that belong to only one set.
notes: A ∩ B means in both sets; A ∪ B means in either or both. The complement of A contains everything in the universal set outside A.
When finding a union, avoid counting the intersection twice: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
For three sets, fill the triple intersection first, then the pair-only regions, then the single-set regions.

reverse-percentage.hint: Identify what percentage of the original amount the stated final amount represents.
notes: An increase of r% multiplies the original by 1 + r/100; a decrease multiplies it by 1 − r/100.
To recover the original, divide the final amount by this multiplier. Subtracting r% of the final amount does not undo an r% increase.

compound.hint: Write the multiplier for one time period, then apply it repeatedly.
notes: After n equal periods, a starting amount P becomes P(1 + r/100)ⁿ for growth or P(1 − r/100)ⁿ for decay.
Use the number of compounding periods as the exponent. To find an unknown rate, divide by P and take the appropriate root.
Do not round between periods. If rates change, use a separate multiplier for each period.

percentage.hint: Decide which amount represents 100% before setting up the calculation.
notes: A percentage of an amount is (percentage ÷ 100) × amount. Percentage change = change ÷ original amount × 100.
Use 1 + r/100 for an increase and 1 − r/100 for a decrease. Successive percentage changes use successive multipliers.
For simple interest, calculate the interest on the original principal for each period; it is not compounded.

direct-inverse.hint: Turn the proportionality statement into an equation containing a constant k.
notes: Direct proportion to x gives y = kx; inverse proportion gives y = k/x. If the statement says x² or √x, keep that power or root in the model.
Use the known pair of values to find k before substituting the new value. Keep the same constant for both situations.
Check the direction of change: for positive inverse proportion, increasing x decreases y.

ratio.hint: Express the quantities as multiples of one common part.
notes: For a total divided in the ratio a : b, one part is total ÷ (a + b). Multiply by a or b to obtain each share.
When linking two ratios, first make the shared quantity the same in both. Do not combine unlike-sized parts.
If some of a share is then used or transferred, calculate that change from the correct share, not from the original total.

standard-form.hint: Separate the number between 1 and 10 from the power of ten.
notes: Standard form is a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ |a| < 10 and n is an integer. Moving the decimal point changes the exponent.
For multiplication or division, operate on the coefficients and use the index laws for the powers of ten. Renormalise the coefficient afterwards.
For addition or subtraction, write both values using the same power of ten first.

recurring.hint: Choose powers of ten that place the repeating block in the same position in two equations.
notes: Let x be the recurring decimal. Multiply by a suitable power of ten, then subtract equations so the recurring tails cancel.
For a non-recurring prefix, align the recurring tails after that prefix before subtracting. Solve the resulting equation and simplify the fraction.

fractions.hint: Rewrite mixed numbers as improper fractions and look for a useful common denominator.
notes: Add or subtract fractions only after giving them a common denominator. For multiplication, multiply numerators and denominators; for division, multiply by the reciprocal.
Cancel common factors, not terms joined by addition. Reduce the final fraction fully.
For a “show that” question, keep exact fractions and write each equality so the stated result follows from your working.

rationalise.hint: Multiply by a factor that removes the square root from the denominator.
notes: For a single square-root denominator, multiply top and bottom by that root. For a binomial denominator a + √b, use the conjugate a − √b.
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² explains why a conjugate removes the root term in the denominator.
Expand carefully, simplify square factors inside roots and reduce the final expression. Keep exact surds rather than decimals.

surds.hint: Look for a square factor inside each square root.
notes: For non-negative a and b, √(ab) = √a × √b. Extract the largest convenient square factor before combining terms.
Only like surds can be added: their simplified root parts must match. Use ordinary bracket expansion when multiplying surd expressions.
Squaring an equation can introduce extra solutions, so check candidates in the original equation.

indices.hint: Write each expression using a common base, then work with the exponents.
notes: For the same non-zero base: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, and (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ.
a⁰ = 1 for a ≠ 0. A negative exponent means a reciprocal; a fractional exponent means a root.
Deal with numerical coefficients separately from the powers of letters. Index laws for products do not apply across addition.

prime-factors.hint: Express the numbers as products of primes before comparing their factors.
notes: Keep dividing by primes until every factor is prime. Index notation records how often each prime occurs.
The HCF uses the smaller power of each shared prime; the LCM uses the largest required power of each prime.
For a perfect square, every prime exponent must be even. For a perfect cube, every exponent must be a multiple of three.

rounding.hint: Round the inputs to the precision requested before performing the estimate.
notes: Significant figures begin at the first non-zero digit. Decimal places count positions after the decimal point.
For an estimate, show the rounded calculation explicitly. Use brackets and follow the order of operations.
A final instruction to round an exact calculation is different: retain full accuracy until the final step.

calculator.hint: Enter the expression in stages, keeping the fraction and any powers inside the intended brackets.
notes: Use brackets around a whole numerator or denominator. Check whether a root or power applies to one term or the entire expression.
Keep the unrounded calculator value until the requested final rounding. If asked for the display, copy the required digits before rounding.

simultaneous.hint: Choose elimination if a variable can be cancelled easily; choose substitution if one variable is already isolated.
notes: For elimination, multiply whole equations to create equal or opposite coefficients. Add or subtract the equations carefully.
For a linear and a quadratic equation, substitute the linear expression into the quadratic. Solve for all possible values and pair each with its corresponding other coordinate.
Check each pair in both original equations.

inequalities.hint: Isolate the variable, watching for a step that multiplies or divides by a negative number.
notes: Solve like an equation, but reverse the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative quantity.
On a number line, use an open endpoint for < or > and a closed endpoint for ≤ or ≥. Integer solutions must satisfy the original inequality.
For a graph region, draw each boundary, test a point and keep the intersection of the allowed half-planes.

quadratic.hint: Move everything to one side so the equation is in the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
notes: Try factorising when the coefficients permit it. Set each factor equal to zero to obtain both possible roots.
Otherwise use x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / (2a), substituting signed values of a, b and c in brackets.
Check whether the context restricts the roots, for example to positive lengths. Round only after calculating both candidates.

linear.hint: Collect the variable terms on one side and the constant terms on the other.
notes: Apply the same operation to both sides. Expand brackets carefully before collecting like terms.
If the equation contains fractions, multiplying every term by a common denominator often makes it easier to solve.
Substitute your value into the original equation to check it. In a word problem, define the variable before forming the equation.

complete-square.hint: First factor the coefficient of x² out of the quadratic terms.
notes: Use x² + px = (x + p/2)² − (p/2)². Any coefficient factored outside the bracket also multiplies the correction term.
Expand your completed-square form to check that all three original coefficients are recovered.

factorise.hint: Check for a common factor before trying a bracket pair.
notes: Take out the greatest common numerical factor and the lowest shared power of each letter.
For a quadratic, seek two factors whose product and sum reproduce the required coefficients. Check for a difference of two squares.
Expand your answer to verify it. “Fully” means no remaining factor can be factorised further at this level.

expand.hint: Multiply one pair of brackets first, keeping every product visible.
notes: Every term in one bracket must multiply every term in the other. Take extra care with negative signs.
Collect like powers only after expansion. If a third bracket or outside factor remains, multiply the entire intermediate expression by it.
Check the leading term and constant term as quick checks on the final expression.

subject.hint: Undo operations around the required letter; if it appears twice, collect those terms before isolating it.
notes: Remove fractions by multiplying both sides by the denominator. Keep brackets around an entire numerator or expression.
If the subject occurs in several terms, move those terms to one side and factor out the letter.
Apply roots or powers only after the relevant expression is isolated. Preserve any restrictions inherited from denominators or roots.

algebra-fractions.hint: Factor the numerator and denominator before trying to cancel anything.
notes: Only common factors may be cancelled. Terms separated by + or − cannot be cancelled individually.
To combine fractions, use a common denominator and multiply each numerator by its missing factor. Put a subtracted numerator in brackets.
State or retain restrictions where an original denominator would be zero.

simplify.hint: Distinguish terms joined by addition from factors joined by multiplication.
notes: Collect like terms only when their letters and powers match. In a product, multiply coefficients and apply index laws to matching bases.
For a quotient, cancel common factors after factorising. A factor cannot be cancelled through an addition sign.
Keep exact fractions or surds if the question requests an exact form.

substitution.hint: Define what each letter represents and substitute values in brackets.
notes: When substituting a negative value, brackets preserve the distinction between −x² and (−x)².
Follow the order of operations. For a worded expression, build the operations in the order described and use brackets where needed.
Check units and whether the result is a formula, an expression or a numerical value.

notation.hint: Identify the role of each number and letter in the expression.
notes: A coefficient multiplies a variable term; a constant term contains no variable. Include the sign belonging to a term.
A power applies to its base. Brackets change what is included in that base.

sequence.hint: Compare consecutive terms before choosing a formula for the pattern.
notes: A constant first difference suggests an arithmetic sequence: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d. Constant second differences suggest a quadratic nth term.
A constant ratio suggests a geometric sequence: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹. Keep the first term at n = 1 when checking a formula.
To decide whether a value belongs to the sequence, solve for n and check that n is a positive integer.

graph-transform.hint: Track one known point and distinguish a change inside f from a change outside it.
notes: If (a, b) lies on y = f(x), it moves to (a, b + k) on y = f(x) + k, and to (a − k, b) on y = f(x + k).
On y = cf(x), the y-coordinate becomes cb. On y = f(cx), the x-coordinate becomes a/c.
Apply the transformation to coordinates, not just to the appearance of the sketch. Changes inside the function affect x in the inverse way.

inverse-function.hint: Write the function as y = …, then reverse the relationship between input and output.
notes: Swap x and y and rearrange to make y the subject. This gives the inverse where the original function is one-to-one.
The inverse undoes the function; it is not 1/f(x). Check by composing the function with its inverse.
Restrictions on the original domain become restrictions on the inverse range, and vice versa.

functions.hint: For a composite function, work from the innermost function outwards.
notes: fg(x) means f(g(x)): first find g(x), then put that entire expression in place of x in f.
Use brackets when substituting an expression. To solve a function equation, form an ordinary equation and apply any domain restrictions.
Check which inputs are excluded by a denominator or square root.

calculus.hint: Differentiate the expression before substituting the point or time requested.
notes: The power rule is d(axⁿ)/dx = anxⁿ⁻¹. Differentiate each term separately; a constant differentiates to zero.
For a stationary point, solve dy/dx = 0, then substitute each x-value into the original function for its y-coordinate.
If s is displacement, ds/dt is velocity and d²s/dt² is acceleration. Distance travelled requires attention to changes of direction.

straight-line.hint: Find the gradient first, then use a point on the line to determine its position.
notes: Gradient = (change in y) ÷ (change in x). Keep the order of the two points consistent in numerator and denominator.
Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) or y = mx + c. Parallel lines have equal gradients; non-vertical perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1.
The midpoint averages the x-coordinates and the y-coordinates separately. Check the final equation using a known point.

motion-graph.hint: Read what each axis measures before interpreting a gradient or an area.
notes: A distance–time gradient gives speed. A velocity–time gradient gives acceleration, and signed area gives displacement.
Split an area under a straight-line graph into rectangles, triangles or trapezia. Convert time units before combining them with speed units.
A horizontal line means constant vertical-axis value; it does not mean the same physical thing on every type of graph.

graphs.hint: Identify the equation and the axis scales, then connect the requested value to a point on the graph.
notes: For a table of values, substitute each x-value carefully, especially negatives and powers. Plot using the stated scale.
Solutions of an equation can be read from intersections: with the x-axis for y = 0, or with another graph for equal expressions.
Use a smooth curve where appropriate. Graph readings are estimates, so report precision consistent with the scale.

vectors.hint: Trace a route between the required points using vectors that are already known.
notes: Reversing a vector changes its sign. For example, AB = OB − OA when OA and OB are position vectors.
For a point dividing a line segment in a given ratio, use the appropriate fraction of the whole segment, taking direction into account.
Parallel vectors are scalar multiples. To establish collinearity, also show that the vectors lie along a line through a shared point.

transformations.hint: Choose a pair of corresponding points and examine how their positions are related.
notes: A translation needs a vector. A reflection needs a mirror line. A rotation needs a centre, angle and direction.
An enlargement needs a centre and scale factor. Draw rays through corresponding vertices to find the centre; compare signed distances from that centre.
Use more than one vertex to check the description. A negative scale factor puts the image on the opposite side of the centre.

construction.hint: Identify the geometric property the required line or locus must satisfy.
notes: Points equidistant from two fixed points lie on their perpendicular bisector. Points equidistant from two intersecting lines lie on an angle bisector.
For a compass construction, use equal radii where required and leave the construction arcs visible.
For a locus satisfying several conditions, keep only the intersection of the permitted regions and use the stated scale.

similarity.hint: Match corresponding sides before writing a scale factor.
notes: If the length scale factor is k, the area scale factor is k² and the volume scale factor is k³.
Take a square root of an area ratio or a cube root of a volume ratio to recover the length scale factor.
For triangle similarity, justify equal corresponding angles. For congruence, use a valid criterion such as SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS.

volume.hint: Break the solid into familiar shapes and distinguish the height from a sloping length.
notes: Prism volume = cross-sectional area × length. Cylinder volume = πr²h; cone volume = πr²h/3; sphere volume = 4πr³/3.
For a composite solid, add the parts or subtract a removed volume. For surface area, count only the surfaces requested; internal joined faces are not exposed.
Use consistent length units before calculating. Volumes use cubic units and surface areas use square units.

sector.hint: Work out what fraction of a full circle the central angle represents.
notes: For an angle θ in degrees, arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr and sector area = (θ/360) × πr².
A sector perimeter includes the two radii as well as the arc. A segment area may require subtracting a triangle from a sector.
Keep π exact when an exact answer is requested.

circle-theorems.hint: Mark the centre, radii, tangents and equal angles before following the angle relationships.
notes: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc. Angles in the same segment are equal.
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
Match each step to the theorem that actually applies to that arc or tangent. Give the geometric reason if requested.

trigonometry.hint: Mark the known sides and angles, then choose a rule that connects them to the required quantity.
notes: In a right triangle, use Pythagoras for sides or SOH–CAH–TOA for a side–angle relationship. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.
For a non-right triangle, an opposite side–angle pair suggests the sine rule. Three sides, or two sides and their included angle, suggest the cosine rule.
For area with two sides and the included angle, use ½ab sin C. Keep the calculator in degree mode and retain extra digits in intermediate results.

polygons.hint: Decide whether to use an interior-angle sum or a complete turn of exterior angles.
notes: The interior-angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°. The exterior angles of a convex polygon sum to 360°.
For a regular polygon, each exterior angle is 360°/n, and the interior angle at the same vertex is supplementary to it.
If angle expressions contain a variable, form an equation using the appropriate relationship before finding the number of sides.

area.hint: Split the outline into familiar shapes and label which lengths are already known.
notes: Rectangle area = length × width; triangle area = ½ × base × perpendicular height; trapezium area = ½ × sum of parallel sides × height.
For a circle, area = πr² and circumference = 2πr. Distinguish radius from diameter.
Add or subtract component areas for a composite shape. For perimeter, count only the boundary lengths, not interior joins.

measures.hint: Write the relationship between the measured quantities and make their units consistent.
notes: Speed = distance ÷ time, density = mass ÷ volume, and pressure = force ÷ area. Rearrange the required relationship before substituting.
Converting area or volume requires squaring or cubing the length conversion factor.
For average speed over a whole journey, divide total distance by total time rather than averaging the separate speeds.

symmetry.hint: Test whether the whole shape coincides with itself after the proposed reflection or rotation.
notes: A line of symmetry divides the shape into mirror images. A rotational symmetry has order equal to the number of matching positions in one full turn.
Check all markings and details of the shape, not just its outer boundary.

angles.hint: Look for a straight line, triangle or pair of parallel lines that connects the known and unknown angles.
notes: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; angles around a point sum to 360°; triangle angles sum to 180°.
With parallel lines, corresponding and alternate angles are equal, while co-interior angles sum to 180°.
Bearings are measured clockwise from north and written with three digits. Mark north lines before relating a bearing to an interior angle.

mean.hint: Convert the mean into a total before dealing with any missing or changed values.
notes: Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values, so the total is mean × number of values.
For combined groups, add the group totals and divide by the combined number of observations. Weight the means by their group sizes.
When an observation is added, removed or corrected, update both the total and the count as required.

statistics.hint: Order the observations, then translate each stated statistic into a condition on the values.
notes: The median is the middle value, or the mean of the two middle values for an even count. The mode is the most frequent value.
The range is maximum − minimum. It uses only the two extremes, unlike the interquartile range.
If several statistics constrain unknown values, use each condition in turn and check that the completed list remains in the stated order.

money.hint: Separate the quantities and their unit costs, then build the total the question asks for.
notes: Use a consistent unit or currency throughout. For a unit rate, divide by the number of units before scaling to a new amount.
For exchange rates, write an equality between the two currencies so the direction of multiplication or division is clear.
Round money at the end unless the context requires whole purchasable items; then interpret any remainder.

integers.hint: Use the definitions of the number types and keep track of signs and order.
notes: Integers include negative whole numbers, zero and positive whole numbers. A square or cube is formed by the corresponding repeated multiplication.
Use brackets when calculating with negatives. On a number line, numbers further right are greater.
Check all stated restrictions, including whether zero or negative values are allowed.
